title: Banner Drone
subject: Evidence
stem:
At a private Christian makers’ fair, Hannah was struck by a banner drone carrying hand-lettered Psalms after Timothy, the drone operator, launched it toward the exhibit hall. Hannah later died from the injury. Lydia, Hannah’s executor, sued Timothy for wrongful death.

At trial, Lydia calls Ruth, a nurse, to testify that the next morning, Hannah said to Ruth, “Timothy launched the banner drone after the marshal dropped the landing flag.” Twelve minutes later, Hannah died.

To lay the foundation for Hannah’s statement, Lydia offers the court an affidavit from Dr. Luke stating that he was the attending physician that morning and that Hannah had said several times that she knew she was about to die.

Is the affidavit properly considered by the court in ruling on the admissibility of Hannah’s statement?
call: Is the affidavit properly considered by the court in ruling on the admissibility of Hannah's statement?

choices.A: No, because statements made under belief of imminent death may be used only in prosecutions for homicide.
choices.B: Yes, because the judge may consider hearsay in ruling on preliminary questions.
choices.C: No, because the affidavit is hearsay and no hearsay exception covers it.
choices.D: Yes, because, although hearsay, the affidavit is a statement of then-existing mental condition.

rightExplanation:
B is correct. The affidavit is being offered to the judge as foundation while the judge decides whether Hannah’s statement is admissible. It is not being offered to the jury as ordinary merits evidence.

Silver Key: lock the layer. The call asks what the judge may consider while ruling, not whether the affidavit is admissible to the jury.

Gold Key: for a preliminary admissibility question, the judge may consider hearsay; Rule 104(a) frees the court from the evidence rules except privilege. That makes the hearsay objection to the affidavit the wrong layer.

c3.text: This choice reaches the correct yes/no result, but by the wrong route. It treats the affidavit as admissible because it supposedly fits a hearsay exception. The call asks whether the judge may consider it as foundation; Rule 104(a), not the exception label, supplies the answer.

c3.text: B is true and responsive. No CLASH or CALL remains.

studentScript: Court-ruling layer. The affidavit is foundation for admissibility. Gold Key: Rule 104(a) lets the judge consider hearsay. Pick B.

B.signal: Matches the court-ruling layer and the Rule 104(a) Gold Key.
B.lawyer: FRE 104(a) permits the court to consider hearsay in preliminary admissibility rulings, except privilege.

C.signal: This choice treats the affidavit as ordinary hearsay needing an exception instead of foundation evidence for the judge.

D.signal: This choice says yes but reaches yes through an exception label attached to the wrong evidence item and layer.
D.lawyer: The affidavit is considered under Rule 104(a), not because the affidavit itself is a then-existing mental-condition statement.

goldKeys.statement: A federal dying declaration is not limited to homicide prosecutions; it may also apply in a civil case when the declarant is unavailable and believed death was imminent.
